title: How to Start a Discipleship Table This Week
excerpt: You do not need a curriculum, a building, or a title. You need a table, a meal, and the willingness to start before you feel ready.
body:
Most people wait their whole lives for permission to make disciples. They wait for a class to certify them, a pastor to commission them, a season of life that finally feels settled. The permission never comes. Jesus did not start a program. He set a table and called twelve men to it, and most of what they learned they learned over food.

A discipleship table is the simplest unit of obedience to the Great Commission you can run from your own home. It is a regular, shared meal where you open the Bible together, pray together, and let your ordinary life become the classroom. That is the whole thing. The rest of this article is just removing your excuses.

## Pick a time and protect it

The table dies in the gap between intention and calendar. So before you do anything else, choose a night. Tuesdays at 6:30. Sunday lunch after church. Thursday breakfast before work. The specific slot matters less than the fact that it is fixed and repeating, because a recurring rhythm is the only kind people can build a life around.

Write it down. Put it in your phone with an alert. Tell your spouse or roommate so the house is ready. A table that floats from week to week is a table no one trusts enough to come back to.

## Keep the food simple

Hospitality is not performance. The moment you decide the meal has to impress, you have made the table about you, and you have also guaranteed you will quit when the week gets hard. Soup. Chili. A pot of pasta. Tacos where everyone builds their own. Cereal, honestly, if that is what gets people in the door.

Romans 12:13 says to practice hospitality, and the word there is closer to "pursue" than "perform." The point is the open door, not the menu. Paul also reminds us that the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17). Feed people enough to keep them, and no more.

## Start small and honest

You do not need a crowd. Two or three is a table. Jesus said where two or three are gathered in his name, he is among them (Matthew 18:20), and he meant it. Begin with the people already in your life: a neighbor, a coworker, a friend from church who is hungry for more than the weekend service gives them.

Do not announce a ministry. Invite a person. "We're going to eat together on Tuesdays and read a bit of the Bible and pray. Come." That is it. Resist the urge to make it sound official. The official version scares people off and inflates you.

## Have a shape, not a script

A table needs a rough shape so it does not dissolve into either small talk or a lecture. Here is one that works for almost anyone:

Eat first, and let it be unhurried. Twenty or thirty minutes of just being human together does more than people think. Then open one passage, a short one, and read it aloud. Ask what it says about God, what it says about people, and what it asks of us this week. Then pray, naming the real things that came up around the table. Then send everyone home before it gets late.

That is the whole evening. Meal, Word, prayer, home. You will be tempted to complicate it. Don't.

## Expect it to feel awkward

The first few weeks will feel thin. Conversations will stall. Someone will say something strange. You will drive to bed wondering if you are any good at this. Good. That feeling is the cost of starting anything real, and it is also evidence that you are not faking confidence you don't have.

I have planted tables that took two months to find their voice. The ones that lasted were the ones where I refused to quit during the awkward stretch. Faithfulness is mostly just continuing to show up after the novelty wears off.

## When you feel unqualified

You are. So was every person Jesus chose. He took fishermen and a tax collector and men who argued about who was greatest, and he did not wait for them to be ready. The qualification for making disciples is not expertise. It is having met Jesus and being willing to introduce him to someone else. The disciples in Acts 4 were called "unschooled, ordinary men," and the thing people noticed was that they had been with Jesus.

You will learn the Bible better by teaching it at a table than you ever did sitting in a pew. The table will disciple you while you disciple others.

## This week

Text two people today. Pick a night in the next seven days. Buy ingredients for one simple meal. Choose one short passage to read aloud, the Gospel of Mark, chapter one, is a fine place to begin. Then set the table and open the door.

The Great Commission was never given to professionals. It was given to people like you, sent into ordinary rooms, with a meal and a Bible and a willingness to start before they felt ready. The room is waiting. So is the command.
